# Black & white photo

- Route: `/tools/black-and-white-photo`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `photo`
- Slug: `black-and-white-photo`

## Summary

A channel-weighted monochrome conversion with six color sliders, a gentle film curve and fine grain, applied on open and adjustable before you export. (Photo editing)

## Details

This page opens Aperture, the Media Manipulator photo editor, on the Black & white panel with the look called Black & white film already applied as a group of three layers: a Black & white layer at its default channel weights, a Curves layer with a gentle S through (0.25, 0.22) and (0.75, 0.78), and a Grain layer at amount 20. The Black & white layer is a channel mixer by hue rather than a plain desaturation: each pixel's gray is a blend between its luma and a weighted value where the weight comes from the six sliders, Reds 40, Yellows 60, Greens 40, Cyans 60, Blues 20 and Magentas 80 by default. Drag Blues down and a sky darkens; drag Reds up and lips and brick lighten. The curve and grain are separate layers you can tune or delete.
### What it does
- Converts every pixel to gray with six channel sliders from -200 to 300 that set how bright each hue family becomes, the same control a darkroom filter gave on film and a desktop editor gives in its black and white panel.
- Applies Black & white film on open: default channel weights, a Curves layer with points (0, 0), (0.25, 0.22), (0.75, 0.78), (1, 1) that lowers shadows and lifts highlights slightly, and a Grain layer at amount 20, size 1, roughness 50.
- Offers High-contrast black & white in the Looks panel as an alternative: Reds 40, Yellows 40, Blues -40 with Contrast +40 and Clarity 25 for a harder look with a dark sky.
- Adds an optional Tint with a hue and a strength so the gray can lean sepia, selenium blue or any other single color without a second layer.
- Keeps the conversion as a layer: mask it to leave one area in color, lower its opacity for a partial desaturation, reorder it under a Curves layer, and export at full resolution.
### How to use it
1. Drop the photo: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, HEIC, AVIF or TIFF. The editor opens on Black & white with the film look already in the stack.
2. Set the channel sliders: Lower Blues to darken a sky, raise Reds or Yellows to brighten skin, raise Greens for lighter foliage; the histogram follows every move.
3. Adjust curve and grain: Edit the Curves layer the look added, change the Grain amount or size in the Detail panel, or delete either layer from the group.
4. Export: JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF or TIFF at the quality you choose; the grain is reproduced exactly on the server from the same seed.
### Supported formats
- Input: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, HEIC, HEIF, AVIF, TIFF, BMP
- Output: JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, TIFF
- The conversion, curve and grain are per-pixel stages; the exported grain is generated from the same seed on the server and matches the reference bit for bit.
- Black and white JPG and WebP exports are usually a third smaller than the color original at the same quality because the chroma planes carry nothing.
### Technical details
- For each pixel the editor takes the HSV saturation S and value V, the BT.709 luma L = 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B, and the hue h. The gray is (1 - S) x L + S x (sum over the six ranges of w_i(h) x k_i / 100) x V, where k_i are the channel sliders and w_i are the standard hue range weights, 1 within 15 degrees of the range center and falling linearly to 0 at 45 degrees with the default Width 30 and Feather 30. A gray pixel has S = 0 and keeps its luma exactly; a fully saturated pure red has S = 1 and becomes Reds/100 x V, so 0.4 at the default, which is level 102.
- The sliders can exceed the natural range: a channel at 300 makes a saturated hue three times its value before clamping, and a negative channel pulls it below zero and clamps to black, which is how High-contrast black & white turns a deep blue sky to pure black.
- The optional tint adds Tint strength / 100 x 0.25 x (hueToRGB(Tint hue) - 0.5) to each channel of the gray, where hueToRGB gives the fully saturated color of that hue. A warm tint at hue 40 and strength 30 on a mid gray of 128 produces (137, 131, 118).
- The Curves layer from the look is a Fritsch-Carlson monotone cubic through its four points sampled into a 256-entry lookup table, so 0.25 maps to 0.22, 0.75 to 0.78 and 0.5 to 0.5 exactly. The Grain layer adds amount / 100 x 0.2 x (noise - 0.5) per pixel, at most 0.02 or about 5 levels at amount 20, with the noise taken from a hash of the pixel position and the seed.
- The preview on your screen is a WebGL2 render of a 1920 px copy on your own GPU; the download is rendered by our server from the full-resolution original with the same channel, curve and grain code. Color stages agree within a mean of 1 and a maximum of 4 levels; the grain hash is shared, so the grain matches exactly.
### When not to use it
A black and white conversion throws away hue, so when the aim is to keep one color and gray the rest, the color pop page keeps the hue information and only desaturates the other ranges. If the photo is already monochrome and merely flat, the curves, levels or contrast pages change its tones without a conversion layer in the way. A faded color image that needs its color back is a saturation or vibrance job. And a sepia or cyanotype wash is a Photo filter or split toning layer on top of this conversion rather than a replacement for it.
### Use cases
- Portraits: Raise Reds and Yellows a little for luminous skin, lower Blues so the background recedes, keep the grain for texture.
- Landscapes with sky: Blues at -40 and Cyans at 20 give the dark sky of a red filter on film; Greens up lightens grass and trees against it.
- Architecture and street: High-contrast black & white with Clarity 25 pulls out edges in stone, concrete and glass.
- Archive and documents: Default weights with the curve removed give a neutral conversion for scans and reproductions.
### FAQ
Q: Why not just set saturation to -100?
A: Saturation -100 maps every pixel to its luma, so colors of equal luma merge. The Black & white layer lets you decide that blue goes darker than red or that yellow goes lighter than green, which separates a sky from a cloud and a lip from a cheek.
Q: What do the default numbers 40, 60, 40, 60, 20, 80 mean?
A: They are the percentages of a saturated color value that each hue family keeps: a pure red becomes 40 percent of its value, a pure yellow 60, a pure blue 20. They match the defaults most desktop editors ship, so a conversion made elsewhere with the same numbers looks the same here.
Q: Can I keep one part of the photo in color?
A: Give the Black & white layer a mask: a Brush component painted over the area to stay colored with Invert on, or a Color range component set to Subtract. The curve and grain layers in the look apply either way unless you mask them too.
Q: Does the grain look the same in the exported file as on screen?
A: Yes, exactly. The grain is a hash of the pixel position and the seed, with no random numbers, and the server uses the same hash on the original pixels. Because the preview is a 1920 px copy, the grain on screen is scaled, but the exported grain is per original pixel.
Q: Can I export a true grayscale file?
A: The export writes three equal channels in an RGB file in the format you pick. A JPG or WebP of a black and white image compresses well because the chroma is empty, so the file is smaller than the color original at the same quality.
Q: How do I get a sepia print instead of neutral gray?
A: Turn on Tint in the Black & white panel and set Tint hue to about 35 to 40 with a strength of 20 to 30. The gray is pushed toward the hue by strength / 100 x 0.25 of the way between the hue color and mid gray, so it stays subtle.
